newsitem.title: THAILAND: Child labour growing problem in Burma - Suu Kyi.
newsitem.headline: Child labour growing problem in Burma - Suu Kyi.

text.p: Democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi said on Thursday more and more children were working as forced labourers in Burma as their impoverished parents could not heed the obligatory call to work free for the military regime.

"Everyone in Burma knows forced labour is a fact," Suu Kyi told Reuters in a telephone interview. "My understanding is that parents have to send (children) as a replacement, because every household is required to send somebody.
"It has escalated in the last year. Last year we started hearing that it was a growing problem, that more and more children were taking the place of their parents."

Suu Kyi was responding to a report just published by U.S.-based Human Rights Watch Asia that said Burma's military government had forced thousands of children as young as 12 to work as porters or day labourers without pay on the construction of roads, railways and bridges.
Government officials were not immediately available to comment on the report.

The 1991 Nobel Peace laureate said she did not think the government specifically looked for child workers, but said they were sent as replacements for parents who could not afford to leave their fields or jobs to do the labour required by the government.
The report alleged that "hundreds, if not thousands" of children had died from beatings, exhaustion and lack of care in recent years because of the military regime's use of forced labour.
"That's very possible," Suu Kyi said. "But I must say I hadn't heard of beatings of children."
"Of course we know that people doing forced labour are beaten if they do not do their job properly, but I haven't heard of specific beatings of children," she said.
Burma's State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) seized power in 1988 after crushing pro-democracy uprisings.
Human rights organisations and Western governments have accused the SLORC of committing human rights abuses including forced labour.
The International Confederation of Free Trade Unions has alleged that 800,000 Burmese have been forced to work without pay or against their will.
Human Rights Watch also said Burma forced children to work as soldiers, saying the strength of the army had doubled to 400,000 troops since 1988.
The report said evidence suggested the recruitment of boys aged 13-15 had contributed to the rise.
"Often, this recruitment is by force, with whole villages or sections of towns being ordered to give a number of boys to the army or face heavy fines," the report said.
Suu Kyi said she had heard that very young boys had been recruited to join the army, but did not have details.
